## Spatial Disorientation

Continuing experimentation focused on the concept of spatial disorientation (SD) in aviation. This study investigated the physiological and cognitive effects of an induced SD illusion during simulated flight using multimodal sensor data. 

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%"}
- Visual and vestibular illusions administered via motion decoupling
- Data acquired included EEG, HRM, NASA-TLX, and flight metrics

A similar analysis approach was utilized after frequentist modeling checks failed. Additionally, this study focused on exploring different priors for model parameters 
:::
::: {.column width="65%"}
![*Fight Simulator*](media/SD/Figure1.png)
:::
::::

::: notes
- Our second case study focuses on SD which while important to aviation safety in its own right, is particulairly interesting due to its cognitive nature
- SD was induced in a flight simulator using visual and vestibular illusions created via motion decoupling.  
- We collected multimodal physiological data: EEG, heart rate metrics, subjective workload (NASA-TLX), and detailed flight metrics.  
- Initial frequentist models failed again due to nonlinearity and dependency issues, so we applied a similar Bayesian modeling approach.  
- This study also explored the effect of different priors on parameter estimation, highlighting the flexibility of Bayesian methods for complex physiological datasets.  
- The goal was to understand how SD affects both cognitive and physiological states during flight, providing insights for adaptive training or cockpit systems.  
:::


## Model Checks

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%"}
\

A limitation of Bayesian General Linear Modeling is the potential bias introduced when using improper priors. All channels passed statistical tests for univariate normality, but failed for multivariate normality.

Two families of distributions were used as priors for HR/RR and posterior predictive checks were conducted to evaluate model fit.
:::

::: {.column width="70%"}
![](media/SD/Figure3.png){.absolute top="200" left="400" width="60%" height="auto"}
:::
::::

::: notes
- One limitation of Bayesian GLMs is potential bias from improper priors, so careful selection is critical.  
- All physiological channels passed univariate normality tests but failed multivariate normality, highlighting dependencies between signals.  
- To address this, we tested two families of distributions as priors for HR and RR channels.  
- Posterior predictive checks were conducted to assess model fit, ensuring that the chosen priors produced realistic simulated data.  
- These checks help validate that the Bayesian model captures the joint structure of multivariate physiological signals.  
- Visualizations show how well posterior predictions align with observed data, providing confidence in model reliability.  
:::


## Model Comparison

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%"}
\

Subsets of EEG/Lifemonitor response variables compared to combined set and use of residual correlation estimated evaluated

- ELPD difference indicates how closely two models differ in their posterior predictions 
- Best model indicated by 0 ELPD difference
- SE difference indicates the difference in standard error between two models
:::

::: {.column width="70%"}
![](media/SD/comparison.png){.absolute top="200" left="400" width="60%" height="auto"}
:::
::::

::: notes
- We compared subsets of EEG and Lifemonitor variables to the full combined set to evaluate model performance.  
- Residual correlations were estimated to account for dependencies between physiological channels.  
- The expected log predictive density (ELPD) difference measures how closely two models’ posterior predictions align.  
- A 0 ELPD difference indicates that the two models perform equivalently.  
- Standard error (SE) differences show the uncertainty in ELPD estimates between models.  
- This comparison helps identify the most informative combination of channels while balancing model complexity and predictive accuracy.  
- The figure illustrates which variable subsets yield the best posterior fit according to ELPD metrics.  
:::


## Final Model Parameters {}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
\

Final model utilized Gaussian priors to allow for estimation of residual covariance. Values of parameters indicate the normalized change in the response variable during SD illusions.

- Horizontal lines indicates mean and 1st quantile for each channel 
- X-axis width for each channel indicates likelihood of the parameter value
- Captures variance and uncertainty in physiological channels changing with periods of SD illusions
:::
::: {.column}
![](media/SD/Figure4.png){.absolute top="200" left="500" width="50%" height="auto"}
:::
::::

::: notes
- The final Bayesian model used Gaussian priors to estimate residual covariances between physiological channels.  
- Parameter values represent normalized changes in each response variable during spatial disorientation (SD) illusions.  
- Horizontal lines show the posterior mean and quantiles for each channel, providing a sense of central tendency and variability.  
- The width of the x-axis distribution for each channel reflects the likelihood of specific parameter values.  
- This visualization captures both the variance and uncertainty in physiological responses during SD events.  
- Overall, it provides a clear picture of which channels are most sensitive to SD and the confidence we have in those estimates.  
:::
